metadata.title: Compressing Neural Language Models by Sparse Word Representations

extraction_notes.note: Parameter-count table, perplexity/memory tables, the baseline list (KN3, LBL5, LSTM-s, LSTM-z variants) and dataset description were not extracted as nodes; only the main empirical claims were kept as numerical claims.
The sparse-code learning tricks (clipping, adaptive alpha_t/beta_t) read partly as a procedure; kept as problem, remark and definition instead of an algorithm since no step sequence is given.
Cited self-normalization property of NCE is stated loosely in one sentence; typed theorem (external) rather than remark.

nodes.name: Embedding, Encoding and Prediction subnets
nodes.statement: In the above models, we can view that a neural LM is composed of three main parts, namely the \texttt{Embedding}{}, \texttt{Encoding}{}, and \texttt{Prediction}{} subnets, as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:sNLM}.
nodes.statement_short: A neural LM decomposes into Embedding, Encoding and Prediction subnets.

nodes.name: Embedding subnet
nodes.statement: The \texttt{Embedding}{} subnet maps a word to a dense vector, representing some abstract features of the word \cite{word2vec}.
differentia: maps a word to a dense vector

nodes.name: Encoding subnet; context/history representation
nodes.statement: The \texttt{Encoding}{} subnet encodes the history of a target word into a dense vector (known as \textit{context} or \textit{history} representation).
differentia: encodes the history of a target word into a dense vector

nodes.name: Prediction subnet (softmax output layer)
nodes.statement: The \texttt{Prediction}{} subnet outputs a distribution of target words as \begin{align} p(w = w_i|h) = &\dfrac{\exp(s(h, w_i))} {\sum_j \exp(s(h, w_j))}, \\ s(h, w_i) = & \trans{\vector{W}_i} \vector{h} + b_i, \end{align} where $\vector{h}$ is the vector representation of context/history $h$, obtained by the \texttt{Encoding}{} subnet.
nodes.statement_short: Softmax over scores $s(h,w_i)=W_i^\top h+b_i$ gives the next-word distribution; $h$ is the context vector.

nodes.name: Softmax next-word distribution
nodes.statement: p(w = w_i|h) = &\dfrac{\exp(s(h, w_i))} {\sum_j \exp(s(h, w_j))},
nodes.label: eq:sNNLM

nodes.name: Linear scoring function
nodes.statement: s(h, w_i) = & \trans{\vector{W}_i} \vector{h} + b_i,
nodes.label: eq:sNNLM:score

nodes.name: Output weights and bias
nodes.statement: $\vector{W} = (\vector{W}_1, \vector{W}_2, \dots, \vector{W}_V) \in \mathbb{R}^{C\times V}$ is the \textit{output weights} of \texttt{Prediction}; $\vector{b} = (b_1, b_2, \dots, b_V) \in \mathbb{R}^{C}$ is the bias (the prior).

nodes.name: Scoring function
nodes.statement: $s(h, w_i)$ is a scoring function indicating the degree to which the context $h$ matches a target word $w_i$.

nodes.name: Vocabulary size and context dimension
nodes.statement: ($V$ is the size of vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$; $C$ is the dimension of context/history, given by the \texttt{Encoding}{} subnet.)

nodes.name: Normalization dominates time complexity
nodes.statement: The normalization factor in Equation~(\ref{eq:sNNLM}) contributes most to time complexity.

nodes.name: Parameters grow linearly with vocabulary
nodes.statement: The number of parameters in the \texttt{Embedding}{} and \texttt{Prediction}{} subnets in neural LMs increases linearly with respect to the vocabulary size, which is large (Table~\ref{tab:no.param}).

nodes.name: Vocabulary split into base and uncommon sets
nodes.statement: We split the vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$ into two disjoint subsets ($\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$).

nodes.name: Base set
nodes.statement: The first subset $\mathcal{B}$ is a base set, containing a fixed number of common words (8k in our experiments).
differentia: containing a fixed number of common words

nodes.name: Uncommon word set
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{V}\backslash \mathcal{B}$ is a set of uncommon words.

nodes.name: Sparse code
nodes.statement: Following most work in the literature \cite{sparse,sparse2}, we represent each uncommon word with a sparse, linear combination of common ones' embeddings. The sparse coefficients are called a \textit{sparse code} for a given word.
differentia: sparse, linear combination of common ones' embeddings

nodes.name: Common-word embedding matrix U
nodes.statement: Suppose $\vector{U}=(\vector{U}_1, \vector{U}_2, \dots, \vector{U}_B) \in \mathbb{R}^{E\times B}$ is the (learned) embedding matrix of common words, i.e., $\vector{U}_i$ is the embedding of $i$-th word in $\mathcal{B}$.

nodes.name: Base set size B
nodes.statement: (Here, $B=|\mathcal{B}|$.)

nodes.name: Natural sparse code of a common word
nodes.statement: Each word in $\mathcal{B}$ has a natural sparse code (denoted as $\vector{x}$): it is a one-hot vector with $B$ elements, the $i$-th dimension being on for the $i$-th word in $\mathcal{B}$.

nodes.name: Sparse code of an uncommon word
nodes.statement: For a word $w\in \mathcal{C}$, we shall learn a sparse vector $\vector{x} = (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_B)$ as the sparse code of the word.

nodes.name: Embedding from sparse code
nodes.statement: Provided that $\vector{x}$ has been learned (which will be introduced shortly), the embedding of $w$ is \begin{equation} \hat{\vector{w}} = \sum_{j=1}^B x_j \vector{U}_j = \vector{U}\vector{x}, \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The embedding of an uncommon word is the code-weighted combination $Ux$ of common-word embeddings.

nodes.name: Sparse code to dense embedding
nodes.statement: \hat{\vector{w}} = \sum_{j=1}^B x_j \vector{U}_j = \vector{U}\vector{x},
nodes.label: eq:sp2dense

nodes.name: Sparse code learning objective
nodes.statement: To learn the sparse representation of a certain word $w$, we propose the following optimization objective \begin{align} \min_{\vector x}\ \ & \| \vector{Ux} - \vector{w} \|_{2}^{2} + \alpha \|\vector{x}\|_1 + \beta |\trans{\vector{1}} \vector{x} - 1| \nonumber\\ &{} + \gamma \trans{\vector{1}} \max \{\vector{0}, -\vector{x}\}, \end{align} where $\max$ denotes the component-wise maximum; $\vector{w}$ is the embedding for a rare word $w\in \mathcal{C}$.
nodes.statement_short: Least-squares fit of $w$ by $Ux$ with $\ell_1$, sum-to-one and nonnegativity penalties.

nodes.name: Sparse coding objective
nodes.statement: \min_{\vector x}\ \ & \| \vector{Ux} - \vector{w} \|_{2}^{2} + \alpha \|\vector{x}\|_1 + \beta |\trans{\vector{1}} \vector{x} - 1| \nonumber\\ &{} + \gamma \trans{\vector{1}} \max \{\vector{0}, -\vector{x}\},
nodes.label: eq:opt_sp

nodes.name: Fitting loss
nodes.statement: The first term (called \textit{fitting loss} afterwards) evaluates the closeness between a word's coded vector representation and its ``true'' representation $\vector{w}$, which is the general goal of sparse coding.

nodes.name: Role of the regularization terms
nodes.statement: The second term is an $\ell_1$ regularizer, which encourages a sparse solution. The last two regularization terms favor a solution that sums to 1 and that is nonnegative, respectively. The nonnegative regularizer is applied as in \newcite{document} due to psychological interpretation concerns.

nodes.name: Clipping replaces the nonnegativity term
nodes.statement: First, we drop the last term in the problem \eqref{eq:opt_sp}, but clip each element in $\vector{x}$ so that all the sparse codes are nonnegative during each update of training.

nodes.name: Re-parametrized sparse code objective
nodes.statement: Concretely, we solve the following optimization problem, which is slightly different but closely related to the conceptual objective \eqref{eq:opt_sp}: \begin{equation} \min_{\vector{x}}\ \ L(\vector{x}) + \alpha_t R_1(\vector{x}) + \beta_t R_2(\vector{x}), \end{equation} where $L(\vector{x}) = \| \vector{Ux} - \vector{w} \|_{2}^{2}$, $R_1(\vector{x}) = \|\vector{x}\|_1$, and $R_2(\vector{x}) = |\trans{\vector{1}} \vector{x} - 1|$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize fitting loss $L$ plus adaptively weighted $\ell_1$ and sum-to-one penalties $R_1,R_2$.

nodes.name: Adaptive-weight sparse coding objective
nodes.statement: \min_{\vector{x}}\ \ L(\vector{x}) + \alpha_t R_1(\vector{x}) + \beta_t R_2(\vector{x}),
nodes.label: eq:opt_sp_trick

nodes.name: Adaptive parameters
nodes.statement: $\alpha_t$ and $\beta_t$ are adaptive parameters that are resolved during training time.

nodes.name: Constant regularization-to-fitting ratios
nodes.statement: Suppose $\vector{x}_t$ is the value we obtain after the update of the $t$-th step, we expect the importance of fitness and regularization remain unchanged during training. This is equivalent to \begin{align} \dfrac{\alpha_t R_1(\vector{x}_t)}{L(\vector{x}_t)} = w_\alpha &\equiv \mbox{const}, \\ \dfrac{\beta_t R_2(\vector{x}_t)}{L(\vector{x}_t)} = w_\beta &\equiv \mbox{const}. \end{align} or \[ \alpha_t = \dfrac{L(\vector{x}_t)}{R_1(\vector{x}_t)} w_\alpha \text{ and } \beta_t = \dfrac{L(\vector{x}_t)}{R_2(\vector{x}_t)} w_\beta, \] where $w_\alpha$ and $w_\beta$ are the ratios between the regularization loss and the fitting loss.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\alpha_t,\beta_t$ so the ratio of each regularizer to the fitting loss stays at a constant $w_\alpha$, $w_\beta$.

nodes.name: Constant alpha ratio
nodes.statement: \dfrac{\alpha_t R_1(\vector{x}_t)}{L(\vector{x}_t)} = w_\alpha &\equiv \mbox{const},
nodes.label: eq:alpha

nodes.name: Constant beta ratio
nodes.statement: \dfrac{\beta_t R_2(\vector{x}_t)}{L(\vector{x}_t)} = w_\beta &\equiv \mbox{const}.
nodes.label: eq:beta

nodes.name: Ratios are easier to specify
nodes.statement: They are much easier to specify than $\alpha$ or $\beta$ in the problem~\eqref{eq:opt_sp}.

nodes.name: True embeddings from word2vec
nodes.statement: To learn the sparse codes, we first train the ``true'' embeddings by {\tt word2vec}\footnote{https://code.google.com/archive/p/word2vec} for both common words and rare words. However, these true embeddings are slacked during our language modeling.

nodes.name: Sparse codes are not tunable parameters
nodes.statement: As the codes are pre-computed and remain unchanged during language modeling, they are not tunable parameters of our neural model. Considering the learned sparse codes, we need only 4--8 values for each word on average, as the codes contain 0.05--0.1\% non-zero values, which are almost negligible.

nodes.name: Compressed Embedding subnet
nodes.statement: By solving the optimization problem \eqref{eq:opt_sp_trick} for each word, we obtain a non-negative sparse code $\vector{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{B}$ for each word, indicating the degree to which the word is related to common words in $\mathcal{B}$. Then the embedding of a word is given by $\hat{\vector{w}}=\vector{U}\vector{x}$.
nodes.statement_short: Each word's embedding is $Ux$ with $x$ its nonnegative sparse code from problem (5).

nodes.name: Compressed embeddings are dense
nodes.statement: We would like to point out that the embedding of a word $\hat{\vector{w}}$ is not sparse because $\vector{U}$ is a dense matrix, which serves as a shared parameter of learning all words' vector representations.

nodes.name: Base output weights and biases
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we let $\vector{D} = \vector{W}_{:,1:B}$ be the output weights of $B$ base target words, and $\vector{c} = \vector{b}_{1:B}$ be bias of the $B$ target words.

nodes.name: Sharing sparse codes between embeddings and output weights
nodes.statement: We claim that it is reasonable to share the same set of sparse codes to represent word vectors in \texttt{Embedding}{} and the output weights in the \texttt{Prediction}{} subnet.
conclusions: it is reasonable to share the same set of sparse codes to represent word vectors in \texttt{Embedding}{} and the output weights in the \texttt{Prediction}{} subnet

nodes.name: Argument for sharing sparse codes
nodes.statement: In a given corpus, an occurrence of a word is always companied by its context. The co-occurrence statistics about a word or corresponding context are the same. As both word embedding and context vectors capture these co-occurrence statistics \cite{Levy:2014wb}, we can expect that context vectors share the same internal structure as embeddings. Moreover, for a fine-trained network, given any word $w$ and its context $h$, the output layer's weight vector corresponding to $w$ should specify a large inner-product score for the context $h$; thus these context vectors should approximate the weight vector of $w$. Therefore, word embeddings and the output weight vectors should share the same internal structures and it is plausible to use a same set of sparse representations for both words and target-word weight vectors.
nodes.statement_short: Heuristic: embeddings and context vectors capture the same co-occurrence statistics, and output weights approximate contexts, so they share structure.

nodes.name: Co-occurrence argument
nodes.statement: In a given corpus, an occurrence of a word is always companied by its context. The co-occurrence statistics about a word or corresponding context are the same. As both word embedding and context vectors capture these co-occurrence statistics \cite{Levy:2014wb}, we can expect that context vectors share the same internal structure as embeddings.
nodes.statement_short: Embeddings and context vectors capture the same co-occurrence statistics (Levy 2014).

nodes.name: Output weights approximate contexts
nodes.statement: Moreover, for a fine-trained network, given any word $w$ and its context $h$, the output layer's weight vector corresponding to $w$ should specify a large inner-product score for the context $h$; thus these context vectors should approximate the weight vector of $w$.
nodes.statement_short: A well-trained output weight scores its contexts highly, so contexts approximate it.

nodes.name: Conclude shared structure
nodes.statement: Therefore, word embeddings and the output weight vectors should share the same internal structures and it is plausible to use a same set of sparse representations for both words and target-word weight vectors.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude a common set of sparse codes may serve both.

nodes.name: Compressed output weights
nodes.statement: Formally, the $i$-th output weight vector is estimated by \begin{equation} \hat{\vector{W}}_i = \vector{D} \vector{x}_i, \end{equation}

nodes.name: Compressed output weight vector
nodes.statement: \hat{\vector{W}}_i = \vector{D} \vector{x}_i,
nodes.label: eq:sp2detector

nodes.name: Compressed output biases
nodes.statement: The biases can also be compressed as \begin{equation} \hat{b}_i = \vector{c} \vector{x}_i. \end{equation} where $\vector{x}_i$ is the sparse representation of the $i$-th word. (It is shared in the compression of weights and biases.)

nodes.name: Compressed output bias
nodes.statement: \hat{b}_i = \vector{c} \vector{x}_i.
nodes.label: eq:sp2detector_bias

nodes.name: Vocabulary-independent parameter count
nodes.statement: In the above model, we have managed to compressed a language model whose number of parameters is irrelevant to the vocabulary size.
conclusions: a language model whose number of parameters is irrelevant to the vocabulary size

nodes.name: Uncompressed-bias variant
nodes.statement: To better estimate a ``prior'' distribution of words, we may alternatively assign an independent bias to each word, i.e., $\vector{b}$ is not compressed.

nodes.name: Uncompressed-bias variant has negligible growth
nodes.statement: In this variant, the number of model parameters grows very slowly and is also negligible because each word needs only one extra parameter.
conclusions: the number of model parameters grows very slowly and is also negligible

nodes.name: Uncompressed bias improves performance
nodes.statement: Experimental results show that by not compressing the bias vector, we can even improve the performance while compressing LMs.
conclusions: by not compressing the bias vector, we can even improve the performance while compressing LMs

nodes.name: Noise-contrastive estimation (NCE)
nodes.statement: NCE generates a few negative samples for each positive data sample. During training, we only need to compute the unnormalized probability of these positive and negative samples.

nodes.name: Normalized LM probability with normalization factor
nodes.statement: Formally, the estimated probability of the word $w_i$ with history/context $h$ is \begin{align} P(w|h; \vector{\theta}) &= \dfrac{1}{Z_h} P^0(w_i|h; \vector{\theta})\nonumber \\ &= \dfrac1{Z_h}\exp(s(w_i,h;\vector{\theta})), \end{align} where $\bm\theta$ is the parameters and $Z_h$ is a context-dependent normalization factor.

nodes.name: Normalized probability via Z_h
nodes.statement: P(w|h; \vector{\theta}) &= \dfrac{1}{Z_h} P^0(w_i|h; \vector{\theta})\nonumber \\ &= \dfrac1{Z_h}\exp(s(w_i,h;\vector{\theta})),
nodes.label: eq:nrm_lang_model

nodes.name: Unnormalized probability
nodes.statement: $P^0(w_i|h; \vector{\theta})$ is the unnormalized probability of the $w$ (given by the SpUnnrmProb layer in Figure~\ref{fig:NCE-regression}).

nodes.name: Z_h = 1 in the base model
nodes.statement: Following \newcite{Mnih:2012tv}, we set $Z_h=1$ for all $h$ in the base model (without \texttt{ZRegression}).

nodes.name: Per-context NCE objective
nodes.statement: The objective for each occurrence of context/history $h$ is \begin{align*} J(\vector{\theta}|h) = & \log \dfrac{P(w_i|h;\vector{\theta})} {P(w_i|h;\vector{\theta}) + k P_n(w_i)} + \\ & \sum_{j=1}^{k} \log \dfrac{kP_n(w_j)} {P(w_j|h;\vector{\theta}) + k P_n(w_j)}, \end{align*} where $P_n(w)$ is the probability of drawing a negative sample $w$; $k$ is the number of negative samples that we draw for each positive sample.
nodes.statement_short: NCE log-odds objective separating the true word from $k$ noise samples drawn from $P_n$.

nodes.name: Overall NCE objective
nodes.statement: The overall objective of NCE is \begin{equation*} J(\vector{\theta}) = \mathbb{E}_h [J(\vector{\theta}|h)] \approx \dfrac{1}{M} \sum_{i=1}^{M} J(\vector{\theta}|h_i), \end{equation*} where $h_i$ is an occurrence of the context and $M$ is the total number of context occurrences.

nodes.name: Instability with Z_h = 1
nodes.statement: Although setting $Z_h$ to 1 generally works well in our experiment, we find that in certain scenarios, the model is unstable. Experiments show that when the true normalization factor is far away from 1, the cost function may vibrate.

nodes.name: ZRegression
nodes.statement: To comply with NCE in general, we therefore propose a \texttt{ZRegression} layer to predict the normalization constant $Z_h$ dependent on $h$, instead of treating it as a constant.
differentia: to predict the normalization constant $Z_h$ dependent on $h$

nodes.name: ZRegression layer formula
nodes.statement: The regression layer is computed by \[ Z_h^{-1} = \exp(\trans{\vector{W}_Z}\vector{h}+b_Z), \] where $\vector{W}_Z\in \mathbb{R}^{C}$ and $b_Z\in \mathbb{R}$ are weights and bias for \texttt{ZRegression}.

nodes.name: NCE probability with ZRegression
nodes.statement: Hence, the estimated probability by NCE with \texttt{ZRegression} is given by \begin{equation*}\nonumber P(w|h) = \exp(s(h,w)) \cdot \exp(\trans{\vector{W}_Z}\vector{h}+b_Z). \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Explicit normalization at test time
nodes.statement: Note that the \texttt{ZRegression} layer does not guarantee normalized probabilities. During validation and testing, we explicitly normalize the probabilities by Equation~\eqref{eq:sNNLM}.

nodes.name: Perplexity
nodes.statement: We take perplexity as the performance measurement of a language model, which is defined by \[ \mathrm{PPL} = 2^{-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log_2 p(w_i|h_i)} \] where $N$ is the number of running words in the test corpus.
nodes.section: 4.3 Quantitative Analysis of Compressed Language Models

nodes.name: ZRegression improves LSTM perplexity
nodes.statement: The {\tt ZRegression} mechanism improves the performance of LSTM to a large extent, which is unexpected.
conclusions: The {\tt ZRegression} mechanism improves the performance of LSTM to a large extent

nodes.name: Two effects of compression
nodes.statement: To explain this phenomenon, we may imagine that the compression using sparse codes has two effects: it loses information, but it also enables more accurate estimation of parameters especially for rare words. When the second factor dominates, we can reasonably expect a high performance of the compressed LM.
